**The SDK now runs on Java 17.** It previously required Java 25, which excluded
every project pinned to an older LTS — most of the Java ecosystem. This release
lowers the floor without lowering the ceiling: on Java 21+ the SDK still runs its
background work on virtual threads, and consumers on 21+ can still pattern-switch
over its sealed types.

Requested in [#3](https://github.com/vidyalai-in/claude-agent-sdk-java/issues/3).

## Upgrading

Nothing to do. The published API is unchanged, and a jar built for Java 17 runs
unmodified on 21 and 25. If your build enforces a minimum dependency bytecode
level, note that the SDK's class files are now major version 61 instead of 69.

## What changed

**The baseline is Java 17**, set as `<release>17</release>` rather than
`source`/`target` — `release` is what actually rejects post-17 JDK APIs at
compile time, so the baseline is enforced by the compiler instead of by
convention.

The Java 25 requirement rested on two things, and neither had to be a
requirement of *your* toolchain:

- **Pattern-matching `switch`** in six internal methods, now `instanceof`
  chains. This is purely internal. `Message`, `ContentBlock`,
  `SDKControlRequestData` and `ThinkingConfig` are still sealed interfaces —
  a Java 17 feature — so if you are on JDK 21+ your own exhaustive pattern
  switches over them keep working and keep their compile-time exhaustiveness.
- **Virtual threads**, now selected at runtime. Every SDK thread and executor
  comes from an internal `Threads` helper that resolves `Thread.ofVirtual()` and
  `Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor` reflectively, once, into `static final`
  method handles. On Java 21+ the behaviour is byte-for-byte what it was. On
  17-20 it falls back to named daemon platform threads.

Thread names are identical on both paths (`QueryHandler-Reader-0`,
`SPCTransport-Stderr-0`, `session-store-0`, …), so thread dumps read the same
way. You can force the platform path on any JDK with
`-Dclaude.sdk.virtualThreads=false`.

Two properties of that fallback are load-bearing rather than cosmetic:

- It stays **unbounded**. `QueryHandler`'s control executor parks a thread for
  the whole duration of an SDK MCP tool call, and the `notifications/cancelled`
  that ends that call arrives as a *separate* control request. Under a bounded
  pool the cancellation would queue behind the call it exists to cancel, and
  deadlock. On 17 the cost is an OS thread per in-flight control request rather
  than a virtual one — never a correctness change.
- Its threads are **daemons**, because virtual threads always are. Anything else
  would turn every SDK thread into a JVM-exit blocker on a 17 runtime.

**`SessionStoreExecutor`'s default is now runtime-dependent.** Still one thread
per task named `session-store-<n>`; virtual on 21+, daemon platform threads on
17-20. Calling `setDefault(...)` overrides it exactly as before.

**The jar declares `Automatic-Module-Name: in.vidyalai.claude.sdk`**, so JPMS
consumers get a stable module name instead of one derived from the filename.

## Also fixed

**Intermittent `cannot find symbol` build failures**, which turned out to be
unrelated to the baseline. The compiler plugin was configured with
`<useIncrementalCompilation>false</useIncrementalCompilation>`. That flag is
inverted: `false` does not turn incremental compilation off, it switches the
plugin to timestamp-based stale-source selection, which gives javac a partial
source set and leans on implicit compilation for the remainder. A file whose own
timestamp has not moved is then never recompiled even when a type it depends on
changed, and any class outside the reference closure of the "stale" files is
never written.

It was visible once you looked: `mvn clean test-compile` reported "Compiling 1
source file" for a module with 47 test sources, and touching a source produced
"Nothing to compile". `SdkVersion.java` kept it armed permanently, since
`templating-maven-plugin` regenerates it every run and it was therefore always
the one file javac was handed.

**A deadlock when listing sessions from a `SessionStore` with a bounded
executor.** Listing fans out one `loadAsync` per session, and the default
`loadAsync` submits to `SessionStoreExecutor`. The fan-out itself ran as a task
on that same executor and then blocked waiting for those loads — waiting on a
slot it was occupying. The default thread-per-task executor hid it; a bounded
one did not, including the `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)` that
`SessionStoreExecutor`'s javadoc offers as an example. Every worker parked and
the call never returned. The loads are now issued from the calling thread, so
the bound still caps concurrency at 16 but parks the caller instead of a worker.

**A racy test assertion**, found by running the suite on 17. Java 17 is the
first configuration where the *whole SDK* runs on platform threads, and
`TranscriptMirrorBatcherTest.receiveLoop_eagerFlushMode_appendsPerFrameBeforeResult`
failed 14 times in 25 runs there. Its recording store collected entries into a
plain `ArrayList` mutated from two executor threads, and it assumed `flush()`
joins an eager drain already in flight. Virtual threads had been winning that
race on 21+. The batcher itself is unchanged; frame coalescing under load is
documented behaviour.

## Keeping it that way

The repository had no build workflow at all before this release — only a
manually triggered publish job — so nothing would have caught a regression.

- **A CI matrix** now builds and tests on JDK 17, 21 and 25 for every push and
  pull request, and asserts the emitted bytecode is class-file version 61. The
  17 leg is the baseline; 21 and 25 cover the runtimes where the virtual-thread
  path is taken, which compiling against the 17 API cannot check.
- **`SealedExhaustivenessTest`** replaces what the compiler used to do for free.
  A pattern switch over a sealed type with no `default` stops compiling the
  moment a subtype is added; an `instanceof` chain quietly falls through to its
  `else`. This test fails on any new permitted subtype and names each dispatch
  site that needs updating.
- **`ThreadsTest`** exercises *both* threading paths regardless of the JDK the
  build runs on, by reloading `Threads` in a throwaway classloader with virtual
  threads disabled — including an assertion that 64 concurrent blocking tasks
  all run at once, which is the property that keeps tool cancellation from
  deadlocking.
